item.title: SBSQ reboot thread
item.description: Please ask your questions in the comments!
item.content:encoded:
Silver Bulletin Subscriber Questions (SBSQ) has been dormant since April. This wasn’t really planned, exactly. SBSQ is a popular feature.

But it’s been a busy year. We launched or re-launched four models in basically six months between COOPER, PELE, FLIPR and ELWAY.1Most of the time, when a Silver Bulletin feature gets stymied, it’s because of other Silver Bulletin work. We’re trying to give you the best experience possible, and sometimes things get triaged.

But it’s time to reboot SBSQ. Please leave questions for SBSQ edition #32 in the comments below. As usual, comments/questions are a privilege for our greatly appreciated paying subscribers.

Subscribe now

1

Just to give you a roadmap, our 2027 model priorities are: 1) building RAPTOR 2.0 (our NBA model). That definitely will not happen before the midterms. We’re hoping to launch it sometime during the forthcoming NBA regular season; 2) extending PELE to European club soccer; 3) rebooting the FiveThirtyEight presidential primary model.

item.title: Why did Ohio stop being a swing state?
item.description: Still Counting EP4 covers the Ohio and Maine Senate races. Plus, we’re reviving Silver Bulletin Subscriber Questions (SBSQ).
item.content:encoded:
I’ll cover this again under “Silver Bulletin news and notes.” But I wanted to alert subscribers that we published a Model Talk on Tuesday night that evidently landed in a lot of people’s spam folders (including mine). We think it’s an important story, providing historical context on midterm elections that helps to explain FLIPR’s increasingly optimistic forecast for Democrats. So I’m going to play one of my “in case you missed it” cards and recommend you check it out.

Subscribe now

We don’t want Still Counting to be solely about the polls and the horse race. And we’ll hopefully have a chance to exhibit the show’s breadth … after the midterms. But for now, we’re in crunch time, with the election less than five weeks away. This week, Clare, Galen and I focused on two key Senate races: Maine and Ohio. We also talked about the minor scandal1 surrounding Mary Peltola’s treatment of her staffers in Alaska. I don’t think any of us expect this to be a major electoral problem for Peltola, but we differed on how newsworthy the story is.

Video above, audio version below. Once again, we are deeply appreciative of your reviews, comments, likes and subscribes.

The context: A blue wave might revive Ohio’s status as a competitive state

Pop quiz. Which Senate seat are Democrats more likely to flip: Ohio or Maine?

This might seem like an easy question. In 2024, Kamala Harris won the Pine Tree State by 7 points, but lost the Buckeye State by 11. If you buy FLIPR’s forecast, though, Ohio is actually the slightly easier pickup for Democrats.

It’s a close call, so don’t necessarily expect this to hold through Election Day. But for now, Sherrod Brown is ahead by 5.0 points in our Ohio polling average, while Troy Jackson is up by a more modest 2.7 points in Maine. FLIPR’s interpretation of the “fundamentals” (especially the presidential voting data I described above) tightens the difference in the advanced versions of our forecast, but not enough to close the gap entirely.

But FLIPR’s forecast is logical enough. In 2018, the previous Trump midterm, Brown won reelection by a healthy 6.8-point margin in a political environment we expect to be similar to what the parties will face this November. Brown lost by 3.6 points in 2024, a considerably worse year for Democrats, but he greatly outperformed Harris, who lost by 11.2. The math here seems fairly simple: the projected swing toward Democrats is considerably greater than Brown’s margin of defeat in 2024. Indeed, a fair percentage of Ohio voters evidently still think that Brown is an incumbent senator. It’s obviously not a sure thing, but this is not one of those forecasts that gives me the keeps-me-up-at-night, existential dread that I might have, say, in Texas.

In Maine, we’re navigating with much less of a reliable roadmap. Not only has Susan Collins massively outperformed the state’s partisan lean in presidential races — Maine hasn’t voted Republican for president since 1988 — she’s also massively outperformed polling averages, particularly in 2020. And Jackson's late replacement of Graham Platner was unusual, though almost certainly an improvement for Democrats given the magnitude of the accusations against Platner.

I owe you a Model Talk on what happens if Democrats lose one of the Senate races in a blue state — either Maine, where they’re on offense, or Michigan (or less likely, Minnesota or New Hampshire2) where they’re defending currently D-held seats. Would this imply that Republicans are almost certain to hold the Senate, or would Democrats still have some backdoor paths? We’ll save that for another time, because today I want to focus on Ohio.

In 2004, an election with interesting parallels to 2024, Ohio was the tipping-point state. John Kerry lost it by 2.1 points, actually slightly narrower than his 2.5-point margin of defeat to George W. Bush nationally. Had Kerry prevailed in Ohio, he would have won the Electoral College.

But Ohio is nowhere near the tipping point now. Barack Obama won it in 2008 and 2012, albeit by slightly less than his national margins of victory. In the three Trump elections, however, Ohio was 10 to 12 points more Republican than the country as a whole. Here’s that data, with a comparison between Ohio and its Big Ten neighbors, Pennsylvania and Michigan.

It’s slightly interesting that Ohio, Michigan and Pennsylvania all moved closer to the national margin in 2024. Nov. 5, 2024 was obviously not a great night for Harris, but one silver lining for Democrats is that the Electoral College vs. popular vote gap declined as compared to 2016 and 2020. Still, all three Big Ten states have become much redder in the Trump Era — but Ohio more so than the others.

After 2016, there was a much-derided journalistic cliché about reporters visiting Trump voters in Youngstown, Ohio diners. But the thing was … that was actually kind of a data-driven project. Youngstown’s Mahoning County voted for Obama by 28 points in 2012. By 2024, it went for Trump by 9 points instead. It seems like a good use of journalistic resources to cover what a swing that large looks like on the ground.

In fact, a belt stretching northeasterly across Ohio from the Kentucky to the Pennsylvania borders has seen some of the biggest red shifts in the country. Central and northwestern Ohio have also swung toward Trump, but by margins that are much more in line with Michigan and Pennsylvania.

There are a few things going on here. Nothing in Michigan (where I grew up) is Appalachian, or otherwise remotely Southern, but southeastern Ohio fits that definition. Then again, considerable parts of Pennsylvania are both literally and culturally Appalachian too, and they haven’t swung as much.

So part of this may also reflect, in a way that’s similar to fellow ex-swing state Florida, a death spiral of sorts stemming from how Democrats have given up on Ohio in presidential elections. (Or at least how Joe Biden and Harris did; Hillary Clinton intensively campaigned there in the closing days of 2016.)

In a way, though, that’s bullish for Brown and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, who has also emerged with a lead over Vivek Ramaswamy in FLIPR’s polling average. Democrats’ voter-targeting efforts are plausibly more efficient and effective than the Republican ones under Trump. In 2020 and 2024, it didn’t make much sense for Democrats to focus resources on Ohio. This year it does: Ohio is currently the third-most likely tipping-point state in the Senate after Texas and Maine, with an 11 percent chance of deciding who wins the chamber.

There are some other factors in play, too. In Ohio, Democrats have lost a massive amount of ground in the southeastern/Appalachian portion of the state — but it also matters that there have been few places in the state, other than Columbus and its northern suburbs, to counteract this. The Philadelphia suburbs have become much bluer, by contrast, and they have much more impact on the statewide vote count because the Philly metro area is about 3x more populous than the Columbus MSA.

In Michigan, Democrats are helped by favorable trends for the party in the western portion of the state. Cities like Grand Rapids are a bit unusual, with a lot of Dutch-American heritage, and they’re highly educated. Meanwhile, up toward Traverse City, the northwestern portion of the Lower Peninsula has become a somewhat hipster-ized and boutique-y getaway destination (and sometimes a primary place of residence) for older college-educated professionals elsewhere in the Midwest.

None of that means Ohio is likely to recover its swing state status in 2028. But whoever gets elected to the Senate this year will serve through the entirety of the next presidency. Democrats have a candidate with a strong electoral track record in Brown, strong enough that he’s almost a quasi-incumbent. A loss there might be just as devastating to the party’s hopes of retaking the Senate as one in Michigan or Maine.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • I’m not sure why Tuesday’s Model Talk landed in many subscribers’ spam folders. It was a meaty, substantive column that has been popular with people who read it. We’re talking with Substack about the issue and hope to have more detail for you within a few weeks. Honestly, Silver Bulletin is in a bit of a weird state right now where about half our traffic comes from the email list and about half from the web.3 Our email open rates are decent-to-good for a mature newsletter, and we think carefully about how many emails to send out — though we have a fair number of readers who are only interested in our sports coverage or who are not at all interested in sports. (If you’re in either of those categories, there’s a guide for you here on how to control what gets sent to your inbox.) But models like FLIPR and ELWAY are explicitly designed with the web in mind; they’re updated frequently and there’s no way to magically revise a chart in something we sent over email. If you seem to be missing Silver Bulletin posts — we’re publishing approximately 3x a week now, plus updating the models basically every day — we’d recommend that you check your spam folder and whitelist us if they’re winding up there. We may have more tips about this in the near future. Email is great for a niche publication, but spam detection algorithms can be fickle and from our perspective, frustrating.

  • We’re now aiming to update our NFL interactives, ELWAY and QBERT, twice a week instead of once a week. Generally, you should look for one update on Tuesday or Wednesday, and then the second on Friday or Saturday, reflecting the results of the Thursday Night game plus current injury and weather reports.

  • For our sports-centric subscribers, we also published the latest update to our NBA Future of the Franchise rankings on Monday.

  • Silver Bulletin Subscriber Questions (SBSQ) has been dormant since April. This wasn’t really a planned outage, but SBSQ got triaged amidst “Wet Hot Model Summer”. (We basically published COOPER, PELE, FLIPR and ELWAY consecutively without much downtime.) We’ve started a thread here to revive SBSQ for October.

For full access to FLIPR and our other models, please consider becoming a paying subscriber.

1

Or “scandal,” depending on your point of view.

2

Both states look more vulnerable at this point than Georgia, where Democrats have an incumbent running in Jon Ossoff, who is way ahead in the polls.

3

And a smaller portion from the Substack App.

item.title: The Democrats’ AI primary is heating up
item.description: The 2028 nomination race begins as soon as the midterms are over. Some Democrats like Gavin Newsom are scrambling to reformulate their positions.
item.content:encoded:
By Eli McKown-Dawson

Here at Silver Bulletin, we’ve been predicting that AI would become one of the most salient political issues for quite some time. That hasn’t happened with the general public quite yet — just 1 percent of respondents in the latest wave of Gallup’s most important problem poll named “advancement of computers/technology” as the nation’s most important issue. But over the past month, political elites have latched onto the issue in a big way, and there are growing signs that voters are following them.

Sure, some politicians, such as Bernie Sanders, had already been focused on AI — and data centers are increasingly making news and widely disliked. But some combination of the Hugging Face incident1, Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon’s comments on existential AI risk, and Dario Amodei’s subsequent essay on “pacing the frontier” have pushed the issue into mainstream political discourse. “Dozens of lawmakers are now touting new proposals to regulate artificial-intelligence models that have stepped up their capabilities,” according to the Wall Street Journal, and House Democrats are now considering creating a select committee focused on AI.

For his part, Donald Trump is something of an “accelerationist” who has called AI safety concerns a hoax. Some of his most memorable recent statements on the subject include “Whoever wins AI, wins!” and “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” He’s also staunchly pro-data center.

But not everyone is so bullish on AI, and with the arguably alarming rate at which the models are improving, this issue is likely to become more relevant before 2028. Whoever wants to be the next president will need to stake out a clear position before primary season kicks off. Those primaries might feel a long way off, but remember, candidates will almost certainly start to announce their bids in early 2027.2

We were originally going to cover what all of the presidential hopefuls were saying about AI in a single article, but with big prospective fields on each side, we’re going to split things by party. On the Democratic side, there’s broad consensus that data centers should pay for their own energy, and that federal regulation and government oversight of frontier labs are needed. The debates are more about how heavily to restrict data center construction and how aggressively to pursue a slowdown.

We’re going to focus on the top eight presidential contenders, as approximately defined by the betting markets and polls.3 To put some numbers on their positions, we’ve scored all eight candidates from 0-10 on two axes.4 The first ranges from pro-acceleration (10) to pro-regulation (0), the second from “Likes to talk about AI” (10) vs. “not much to say on the issue” (0). We’ll show each candidate's scores in their section, and include a chart for all eight candidates at the end of the post.

Silver Bulletin is a reader-supported publication. For full access to our midterms model as well as to our other AI coverage, consider becoming a subscriber.

Gavin Newsom

Acceleration: 4.5

Salience: 7.5

We’ve written about Newsom’s declining primary fortunes: he’s dropped from 37 percent in the markets last November to around 15 percent today. But he’s uber-ambitious, so there’s a good chance he’ll still run — unless, he claims, Kamala Harris jumps into the race. If he does enter the primary, Newsom will likely position himself as a leader on the AI issue due to his experience governing the state that houses the major American labs.

But in his continuous quest to optimize his political profile, Newsom has somewhat flip-flopped as the public has polarized against data centers and AI more generally.

In 2024 alone, Newsom signed 17 AI-related bills into law. But he also vetoed SB 1047, an ambitious bill supported by many people in the AI safety space, which would have created whistleblower protections and required risk assessments from developers of the most powerful AI models. And in 2025, Newsom vetoed legislation that would have required data centers to track their water usage, a move that Trump might approve.

But fast forward one year, and he’s criticizing Trump and the federal government for doing too little to regulate AI and positioning California as a regulatory trendsetter. “The federal government’s abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation,” he said in a recent press release.

Last year, Newsom also signed a new bill, SB 53, which had many similarities to SB 1047. It required frontier labs to publish transparency reports, disclose critical safety incidents, and maintain anonymous channels for whistleblowers. More recently, he signed a slew of bills that gave local officials more authority to monitor data centers, established a framework for independent safety evaluators, and created a state registry of AI auditors. On X, he said: “We’re making sure these companies pay the costs they create instead of sticking working families with the bill.” He also issued an executive order last month to explore, among other things, creating a “kill switch” for the most advanced models.5

Still, few other Democrats on this list have Newsom’s track record of opposing major AI regulations in the past.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

Acceleration: 1

Salience: 6

The markets are getting more bullish on an AOC primary win, although in a recent New York Times interview, she said she’ll make a decision on running after the midterms. But AOC’s AI positions have been quite consistent. Across a number of bills, she’s been Sanders’ House counterpart on the pause/moratorium side of the AI and data center debate. She signed on to Sanders’ recently proposed bill that would ban artificial superintelligence and co-led the introduction of a bill that would halt new data center construction until more federal safeguards were put in place.

Her press release when that bill was announced read, in part, “Congress has a moral obligation to stand with the American people and stop the expansion of these data centers until we have a framework to adequately address the existential harm AI poses to our society.” In addition to highlighting ICE’s use of AI, AOC has focused in on the privacy angle:

“We must sound the alarm now — because this surveillance of the American people is not going to stop. We must stop it. All of this harm has occurred, not in spite of, but because of the absence of federal legislation to regulate AI.”

On the same front, she authored the DEFIANCE Act, a bipartisan bill that would allow people depicted in explicit deepfakes to take civil action against the creators or distributors of those images. And just last week, she unveiled a new bill, along with Sanders and Jeff Merkley, that would prohibit federal use of license plate readers and cut off federal grants to state and local governments that use them.

AOC is also concerned about a potential AI bubble and said in an email to supporters that “We must make it clear now that should the A.I. bubble pop, Congress should not bail out Big Tech.” She also thinks that the “biggest threat to humanity are the tech oligarchs themselves.” We’d argue that there’s some tension between being concerned that AI is a bubble, which can imply skepticism about AI capabilities, and putting a premium on safety concerns. This is a subtlety that could split the left from the center in the primary.

Jon Ossoff

Acceleration: 3.5

Salience: 5.5

While Ossoff is getting just 8 percent support in the primary polls, on average, he’s had a recent surge in prediction markets. In 2023, he chaired a hearing on AI and human rights, but Ossoff’s foray into the data center policy debate has been more recent. Back in January, Axios reported that he hadn’t “veered into [the data center] issue — yet.” But a few months later, he launched an inquiry into whether data centers are increasing Georgia power bills. Ossoff still touted the “over $4.5 billion in AI-related venture capital investments” flowing into the state, but his concern was that, “without proper safeguards, higher prices and capital costs from increased energy generation could be passed onto Georgia families.”

That’s a fairly measured approach as compared to some of the other presidential hopefuls you’ll see on this list. But after the ongoing bout of concerning behavior from frontier models, Ossoff has become one of the more safety-focused Democrats. At a recent rally, he said:

“A capable president would move swiftly to secure and reassure the American people. Rush inspectors into frontier labs, fortify the nation against bioterrorism, demand legislation from Congress and lead the world toward an AI treaty.”

Ossoff also criticized Trump’s more laissez-faire approach: “They’ve invested heavily in AI labs. They’ve invested heavily in data centers. So, the first family has a financial stake in this industry, and as a result, the president of the United States is compromised.” At the same time, he was one of four Senate Democrats who voted to advance the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill “aimed at pressuring state utility regulators to reduce data center-related costs,” according to Roll Call. Additionally, in August, Ossoff announced an investigation into risks AI could pose to children.

Kamala Harris

Acceleration: 4

Salience: 4

It’s still unclear whether the former vice president will throw her hat in the ring again. But given her near-universal name recognition, Harris would at least be a serious early contender, especially with South Carolina kicking off Democrats’ primary calendar. She’s currently leading in the Race to the WH primary polling average, though prediction markets are more skeptical about her chances.

Harris was the Biden administration’s unofficial AI czar. Despite that, she’s had less to say about the issue than some of the other contenders and has generally taken a middle-of-the-road approach relative to her Democratic peers. In a 2023 London speech, she said that “President Biden and I reject the false choice that suggests we can either protect the public or advance innovation; we can and we must do both.” At the same time, she warned that “when people around the world cannot discern fact from fiction because of a flood of A.I.-enabled mis- and disinformation, I ask: Is that not existential for democracy?” She also announced the US AI Safety Institute — now renamed the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence — in the same speech.

Then last month, Harris joined other Democrats in calling for more government regulation of AI and a slowdown of frontier development, including independent federal oversight and treaties with other countries to prevent dangerous uses of AI:

“The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development. A slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest.”

But still, she said that a slowdown “does not mean giving up on this technology’s potential to produce life-saving benefits in fields like medicine.” And Harris endorsed Project Blueprint, a project led by Democratic megadonor and venture capitalist Ron Conway to “assert influence over national AI policy.” As Nate wrote, this is an arguably slightly “weird read” on the public’s mood, treating AI as more of a “normal technology” that will be regulated through competing, partisan lobbying efforts.

Andy Beshear

Acceleration: 4

Salience: 4.5

The markets like Beshear relative to his current standing in the polls. Like Newsom, he’s had some opportunities to deal directly with data centers as a governor. Beshear has been more consistently pro-regulation, but isn’t for an outright ban. Back in June, he said “Any data center that wants to look at Kentucky is going to have to pay for 100 percent of its own energy.” He’s also said that they must pass all of Kentucky’s environmental rules and “need to be able to tell the community, and then prove to us, that they’re not going to have environmental harms.”

Originally, these restrictions took the form of pledges made to Beshear by developers. A Kentucky bill that would have required data centers to cover their own costs got stalled in the state Senate. But in early August, Beshear signed an executive order mandating that data center developers meet the above standards.

Prior to the recent round of AI news, he hadn’t said much about frontier models. But last month he joined other Democrats in calling for increased federal oversight — although with an equivocal statement that also touted the technology’s ability to make medical breakthroughs.

“AI plus CRISPR could solve every genetic disease that we know of in our lifetime, and that’s something we all want to see. But it could also cause huge job displacement. It could create national security concerns, so we have to address it.”

Still, he did call for strong federal oversight and negotiations with China on an AI agreement. A spokesperson for Beshear told the New York Times that Beshear “supports legislation that would require A.I. companies to grant the government real access to provide effective oversight.”

Pete Buttigieg

Acceleration: 4

Salience: 6

Buttigieg has hovered around 5 percent on the markets for some time. Compared to others in his party, he was relatively early to comment on potential AI-driven economic shocks. In June 2025, in a Substack post titled “We are Still Underreacting on AI,” Buttigieg compared the changes brought about by AI to “the Enlightenment or the Industrial Revolution” and said that

“Each facet of life will become very different — and the biggest difference of all is that this time, the changes will play out not over the course of generations but rather in less time than it takes an American student to complete high school.”

In an NPR interview around the same time, he said “the economic implications are the ones that I think could be the most disruptive, the most quickly. We’re talking about whole categories of jobs. Not in 30 or 40 years, but in three or four, half of the entry level jobs might not be there.”

Buttigieg has been comparatively light on discussing data center regulation, but he is concerned about wealth concentration. His signature proposal is an AI dividend, where everyone in the country would receive a share of the profits from major AI labs. “Why shouldn’t we all get a share [of the value created by AI] instead of it going to a handful of super wealthy people who are consolidating their power?” he said on a 2025 podcast.

But Buttigieg does seem to take the risk from frontier models seriously. Earlier this year, he said that AI required “a new social contract” and in September, he said “There needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI.”

Josh Shapiro

Acceleration: 5

Salience: 5.5

Like Buttigieg, Shapiro is also hovering around 5 percent on the prediction markets, but he’s actually trailing Buttigieg in the polls. The Pennsylvania governor’s evolution on data centers over the past few years looks strikingly similar to Newsom’s. Back in 2024, Shapiro touted AI investment in Pennsylvania, and in 2025, he announced that the state was “all in on AI.” “This is what a united front looks like to win the battle of AI supremacy,” he said after Amazon chose to build two datacenter campuses in PA.

But earlier this year, he released new guidelines for data center developers in the state, who must commit to “bringing their own power generation… strict transparency standards and direct community engagement… [and to] hire and train local workers.” A few months later, he described data center companies as “greedy” and “predatory” and signed an executive order that tied previous voluntary standards to tax benefits and expedited permitting:

“I’m here to say today that we will not be bullied by these developers. We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers for these big tech companies. We have a long history in Pennsylvania of industry running roughshod over our communities to make a buck. That stops with me.”

On the models front, Shapiro recently called for more regulation: “I want to be clear: I am not a doomer. I don’t think it is inevitable that AI is going to take over the world or that someone will misuse it to kill us or do harm. But I do have real concerns… I’ve called on the federal government to step up and regulate the AI industry.” And earlier this year, his administration also sued Character.AI, alleging that one of their chatbots claimed to be a licensed medical professional in Pennsylvania.

Mark Kelly

Acceleration: 6

Salience: 7

The last candidate on our list, Kelly has been one of the more legislatively active Democrats on AI — and one of the more bullish on the technology. In September, he told Politico “I do believe there are benefits, and they could be significant. I also see the national security implications of not getting this right and not being the leader. This thing can blow up on us — not literally, but blow up metaphorically — at any moment and cause some real damage. We want to be ahead of it.”

Back in 2025, Kelly released an AI for America plan “that would require tech companies to contribute to a fund intended to help society adjust to the technology’s impact on jobs, infrastructure and the environment.” And last month, he proposed the Make AI Work for Americans Act that would support workers as AI changes the economy, funded through taxes on excess profits, digital advertising, and AI usage.

“These companies are getting rich off of a technology trained on the wealth of humanity’s research, knowledge, and work — our ideas and discoveries. My bill would require them to give some of that wealth back to us by investing in the American worker through an AI Horizon Fund.”

Aside from worker protections, Kelly joined other Democrats in criticizing Trump’s hands-off approach: “While the people inside the industry discuss catastrophic damage and the chance that AI, and I quote, ‘will kill us all by the end of the decade,’ the White House is actively lobbying against regulation.” Still, Kelly has played up race dynamics with China more than most Democrats, recently saying “we can’t allow the Chinese to win the race to getting the best AI technology. That would be a mistake.” He also introduced a bill that would direct the NSA to “develop and disseminate security guidance to protect America’s advanced technology from foreign adversaries.”

Finally, here’s the chart we promised with every candidate’s scores. We’ll add the Republicans after the second installment of this story.

Share

1

A weirdly euphemistic way to refer to a hack.

2

In January 2019, Tulsi Gabbard, Julián Castro, Kirsten Gillibrand, Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg, and Marianne Williamson entered the Democratic primary.

3

Kalshi and Polymarket have an identical top eight as of Tuesday afternoon, albeit with different win probabilities. Seven of those eight appear in the Race to the WH Democratic primary polling average. The one disagreement is Cory Booker. Race to the WH has him slightly above Andy Beshear in the polls, while the markets have Booker far lower than Beshear.

4

These are my scores, but I did have three AI models — Claude Fable 5.1, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and GPT-6 Astra — code the candidates on these axes as a baseline prior.

5
